items.originalEnglish: As a child, I wanted to be an architect. That instinct never really left.

items.originalEnglish:
That early interest in design stayed with me when I chose to study software engineering. Frontend became my creative space: a place where code could become something people could see, interact with, and make their own.

I care about the character of what I build. The shape of an interface, the rhythm of its interactions, and the clarity of its next step all influence how it feels to use. Software gave me a different medium for that same desire to create.

items.originalEnglish: Enterprise frontend work gave my interest in design a practical setting. An interface sits within a larger application, with requirements and people depending on it. That context remains part of how I approach the experiences I build today.
items.english:
Enterprise frontend work at Allianz Technology gave my interest in design a practical discipline. A single screen is never an island; it lives inside a larger application with strict requirements, shared standards, and real users relying on it.

Collaborating across teams in Munich and Bangkok taught me to look beyond surface polish. The quiet details a user never consciously notices are often the ones an engineer has to get right.

My role lived inside a shared delivery effort—listening closely to what stakeholders actually needed, translating those requirements into frontend architecture, and building alongside engineers across locations.

When squads work across different places, shared clarity matters just as much as clean code. It trained me to see the whole structure first, so the piece I owned would fit naturally into everyone else’s.

I started with the work in front of me: bringing GPT into Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket workflows, with people reviewing the outputs. The possibility I had imagined began to present real problems I had to work through.

items.originalEnglish:
Some people around me, including others working in the same field, were not yet convinced by AI. I could see its possibility. Making that possibility useful meant facing the problems myself, one after another.

The skills and workflows I build come from those encounters. I work through a problem, reflect on what it taught me, seek better methods, and return to the next version. Week after week, that effort becomes HolyMind.
items.english:
Even peers in the same discipline were unconvinced—and fairly so, while the idea existed mostly in theory. To make it tangible, I started building on my own, working through each obstacle one piece at a time.

Every skill and workflow I create traces back to those hands-on encounters. I test an approach against a real problem, examine where it breaks, look for sharper methods, and return to refine the next version. Week after week, that steady cadence became HolyMind.

I let the experience settle, then look outward. I research approaches, ideas, and tools from around the world, selecting and combining the strongest methods I can find for the problem in front of me.

A skill gradually earns its own purpose, method, and character. That is the moat I am working to build: accumulated experience, careful selection, and repeated refinement. Connected into workflows, those capabilities become a larger way of working.
items.english:
Once a lesson holds up in practice, I look outward. I study research, engineering patterns, and tools from around the world, selecting and combining the strongest methods I can find for the problem in front of me.

Through repeated testing and trimming, each skill earns its own purpose, method, and character. Connected into workflows, those capabilities give new work a stronger foundation from the start.

That is the moat I am building: not a secret shortcut, but lived experience, deliberate curation, and revision after revision until a capability proves its worth in real use.

items.originalEnglish:
The AI era gives my frontend instincts and software engineering background a wider creative space. I can shape a tool’s capabilities and the way someone enters, understands, and uses it.

I want the next step to feel clear, the interaction to feel inviting, and the person using it to feel in control. The aim is an experience people want to return to in their own work. Beautiful design can make depth approachable, while keeping the reasoning, sources, and moments for human review within reach.
items.english:
Working with AI brings my frontend instincts and software engineering background together in a wider creative space. I can shape both the underlying machinery of a tool and the way someone enters, understands, and works with it.

The interface should absorb the heavy complexity behind the scenes while keeping the next step clear, the interaction inviting, and the person in control. Reasoning, sources, and moments for human review remain within reach whenever they are needed.

Thoughtful design opens the door, but care in every detail of use is what makes people want to return. To me, that is the heart of AI experiences.
